answer:
No—an exact, universally accepted numerical count of the number of grains of sand on Earth has not been published by an authoritative scientific organization or peer-reviewed study; the sources found only report order-of-magnitude estimates, not an exact figure [S3][S6][S12].  

Yes—scientific consensus (as reflected in how these estimates are constructed) does not treat an exact count as well-defined or knowable, because the result depends on definitions and assumptions such as what counts as “sand grains” (grain size range), where to measure them (beaches only vs. all sand in Earth’s crust/sediments), and the implied average grain dimensions and distribution [S12][S6][S3].  

Best-available quantitative estimate from reputable sources (with assumptions/range): the commonly cited estimate is on the order of **~7.5 × 10¹⁸ grains** of sand (often phrased as “seven quintillion, five hundred quadrillion”), associated with the “beaches and deserts” style calculations; this is the figure repeated by NPR’s “Krulwich Wonders” discussion of the estimate [S6]. A separate, more explicitly assumption-driven calculation for **sand in the crust** gives a much larger number: **~4 × 10²⁷ sand grains**, assuming an average sand-grain diameter of **250 micrometers** [S12].
